To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
vaccination of cattle with a single FMDV serotype induces a cross-reactive T cell repertoire, but the magnitude of this response varies between animals.
vaccination with whole FMDV induced a serotype-cross-reactive proliferative immune response in cattle.
vaccination with FMDV or recombinant VP induces cross-reactive proliferating T cell responses in cattle.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the cellular immune response of cattle to foot-and-mouth virus and the role of the T cell response in immunity.
the cellular recognition of foot-and-mouth virus by cattle and its relationship to immunity.
a better understanding of the role of T cells during FMDV infection and vaccination and the development of improved vaccine candidates.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
T cell immunity to FMDV and VP1 is weak in cattle and that the cellular response does not appear to be of major importance to the overall immune response.

vaccination with a single FMDV serotype induced a cross-reactive T cell repertoire that was serotype-specific when tested with purified VP1, but that was not protective against challenge with a heterologous serotype.
the proliferative T cell response is a useful marker of FMDV exposure, but not necessarily of protection.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the cellular immune response to FMDV is weak and that it does not contribute substantially to protection from disease.
T cells are important in the control of foot-and-mouth-disease virus infection and vaccination.
the T cell response to FMDV and VP1 is weak compared to the humoral response, but that vaccination can induce a cross-reactive proliferating T cell repertoire.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the cellular response to FMDV is complex and may vary with the route of infection and the serotype of virus used.
the cellular response to FMDV and VP1 does not appear to contribute to protection and is not a reliable indicator of immunity to FMDV.
T cells do not play a major role in the control of foot-and-mouth infection.
